summary.text: A male infant born at 41 weeks with a normal newborn exam and newborn screen presented to the pediatrician at 2 months of age with a week of loose stools and a total weight gain of 36 g since birth, with malnutrition noted. He was exclusively breastfed and received vitamin D; family history was negative for renal or adrenal disease.

At the community hospital sodium was 120 mmol/L and potassium 6.9 mmol/L; he was transferred to the PICU in compensated shock and received 40 mL/kg saline during transport and further volume and red blood cell resuscitation. After resuscitation, endocrine studies, a high-dose cosyntropin stimulation test and urine studies were obtained; aldosterone was 315.9 ng/dL while the cosyntropin response was appropriate and 17-hydroxyprogesterone and renin were reported normal.

Urine studies were consistent with a urinary tract infection (E. coli, 20,000 cfu/mL); he was started on ceftriaxone, switched to cephalexin on hospital day 3, and later put on sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim prophylaxis. Renal ultrasound showed a markedly dilated, tortuous left ureter with caliectasis and bladder-wall thickening.

On hospital day 3 the left foot was dusky with decreased capillary refill; the left femoral arterial line was removed and Doppler showed a nonocclusive left external iliac thrombus, attributed by the authors to arterial line placement. Hematology recommended enoxaparin, which was later discontinued after the thrombus resolved.

Electrolytes normalized by hospital day 2 and he was discharged with good weight gain and no growth on subsequent urine cultures. Three weeks after discharge aldosterone had normalized (5.1 ng/dL) and electrolytes remained normal; he was diagnosed with transient secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism in the setting of a UTI. Follow-up VCUG showed no reflux or obstruction, left hydroureteronephrosis remains stable, and he is now at the 18th percentile for weight and growing well.
